# sysutils_logrotate (Resource)

Manages a logrotate drop-in file in `/etc/logrotate.d`, below the provider's `root_dir` if that is set, holding one block that rotates the log files in `paths`. The file is written atomically with mode `0644`, owned by the user running Terraform (root), under the provider's shared-file lock, and is checked with `logrotate -d` before it is renamed into place when logrotate is installed. It is removed on destroy. Requires root privileges, unless used with `root_dir` on a tree you can write.

It covers the same ground as a `template` task for `/etc/logrotate.d` in Ansible, or the `logrotate::rule` type of Puppet's logrotate module. Each resource owns one file, `/etc/logrotate.d/<name>`, with one block of log paths.

## Example Usage

```terraform
# Rotate the logs of myapp daily, keep two weeks of them compressed, and
# tell the service to reopen its log files afterwards. Writes
# /etc/logrotate.d/myapp, checked with "logrotate -d" first.
resource "sysutils_logrotate" "myapp" {
  name          = "myapp"
  paths         = ["/var/log/myapp/*.log"]
  frequency     = "daily"
  rotate        = 14
  compress      = true
  delaycompress = true
  missingok     = true
  notifempty    = true
  sharedscripts = true

  # A fresh, empty log file right after rotation.
  create_mode  = "0640"
  create_owner = "myapp"
  create_group = "adm"

  postrotate = <<-EOT
    systemctl kill --signal=HUP --kill-whom=main myapp.service
  EOT

  # Anything the typed attributes don't cover, one directive per line.
  extra_directives = [
    "maxsize 100M",
    "dateext",
    "su myapp adm",
  ]
}
```

<!-- schema generated by tfplugindocs -->
## Schema

### Required

- `name` (String) Name of the file in `/etc/logrotate.d`, such as `"myapp"`. Must consist of letters, digits and `_.+@-`, must not start with `.`, `+`, `@` or `-`, and must not end with an extension logrotate skips, such as `.bak`, `.disabled`, `.dpkg-old`, `.rpmsave` or `~`. Changing this forces a new resource.
- `paths` (List of String) The log files to rotate, as absolute paths that may contain the glob characters `*`, `?` and `[...]`, such as `"/var/log/myapp/*.log"`. Paths with spaces are written in double quotes. Paths must not contain quotes, backslashes, `{`, `}`, `#`, `//`, `.` or `..` components. With `root_dir`, they are written as given: they name the files of the system that boots from the tree.

### Optional

- `compress` (Boolean) `true` writes `compress` (compress rotated files with gzip), `false` writes `nocompress`. If unset, neither is written and the global setting of `/etc/logrotate.conf` applies.
- `create_group` (String) Group of the log file created after rotation. Requires `create_owner`.
- `create_mode` (String) Writes `create <mode> <owner> <group>`, so that an empty log file with this mode, such as `"0640"`, is created right after rotation. `create_owner` and `create_group` are optional, but must be set together: logrotate 3.22 and later read `create <mode> <owner>` as an owner and a group. If unset, no `create` directive is written; use `extra_directives` for `nocreate` or a bare `create`.
- `create_owner` (String) Owner of the log file created after rotation. Requires `create_mode` and `create_group`.
- `delaycompress` (Boolean) `true` writes `delaycompress` (compress each file only at the rotation after the one that created it, for programs that keep writing to it for a while), `false` writes `nodelaycompress`. If unset, neither is written and the global setting of `/etc/logrotate.conf` applies.
- `extra_directives` (List of String) Further directives, one line each, written verbatim after the typed ones, such as `"maxsize 100M"`, `"dateext"` or `"su root adm"`. A directive must not conflict with a typed attribute that is set (such as `"nocompress"` with `compress`), must not be a comment, and must not start a script or contain `{` or `}`; scripts other than `postrotate` are not supported.
- `frequency` (String) How often to rotate: `"hourly"`, `"daily"`, `"weekly"`, `"monthly"` or `"yearly"`. `hourly` needs logrotate to run hourly, which it does not by default. If unset, the global setting applies.
- `missingok` (Boolean) `true` writes `missingok` (a missing log file is not an error), `false` writes `nomissingok`. If unset, neither is written and the global setting of `/etc/logrotate.conf` applies.
- `notifempty` (Boolean) `true` writes `notifempty` (empty log files are not rotated), `false` writes `ifempty`. If unset, neither is written and the global setting of `/etc/logrotate.conf` applies.
- `postrotate` (String) Shell script to run after rotation, written between `postrotate` and `endscript`, such as `"systemctl kill -s HUP myapp.service"`. It is written verbatim, followed by a newline if it does not end with one, and must not contain a line `endscript`.
- `rotate` (Number) How many rotated files to keep (`rotate <count>`). `0` removes old versions instead of keeping any, `-1` never removes them. If unset, the global setting applies.
- `sharedscripts` (Boolean) `true` writes `sharedscripts` (run `postrotate` once for all matching files rather than once per file), `false` writes `nosharedscripts`. If unset, neither is written and the global setting of `/etc/logrotate.conf` applies.
- `validate` (Boolean) Whether to check the new file with `logrotate -d` before it is installed, if logrotate is installed on the host; without logrotate the file is installed unchecked. If logrotate reports an error in the file, apply fails with its output and the file on disk is left as it was. Errors about the log files themselves, such as missing ones, are not errors in the file and are ignored. Below the provider's `root_dir` the check is skipped: logrotate would look up the users, groups and log files of the host rather than of the tree. Defaults to `true`.

### Read-Only

- `content` (String) The rendered file. Refresh reads the file, so any change made outside Terraform shows up as a planned change to this attribute, which apply reverts.
- `group` (String) Group of the file; the primary group of the user running Terraform after apply. A different group on disk shows up as drift.
- `id` (String) Resource identifier (equal to `name`).
- `mode` (String) Mode of the file; always `"0644"` after apply. A different mode on disk shows up as drift: logrotate ignores files writable by group or others.
- `owner` (String) Owner of the file; the user running Terraform (`"root"`) after apply. A different owner on disk shows up as drift: logrotate ignores files owned by other users.
- `path` (String) Path of the file, `/etc/logrotate.d/<name>`.

## The Drop-in File

The example above writes:

```
# Managed by Terraform (sysutils_logrotate). Manual changes will be reverted.
/var/log/myapp/*.log {
    daily
    rotate 14
    compress
    delaycompress
    missingok
    notifempty
    create 0640 myapp adm
    sharedscripts
    maxsize 100M
    dateext
    su myapp adm
    postrotate
systemctl kill --signal=HUP --kill-whom=main myapp.service
    endscript
}
```

- The typed directives come first, in the order above, then `extra_directives` in the order given, then the `postrotate` script. The script is written exactly as given, so a here-document in it keeps working.
- Every typed attribute is optional. An attribute that is not set writes nothing, so the global setting in `/etc/logrotate.conf` applies. For the boolean attributes, `false` writes the opposite directive (`nocompress`, `nodelaycompress`, `nomissingok`, `ifempty`, `nosharedscripts`), which overrides a global setting.
- `extra_directives` may use the directives of a typed attribute only while that attribute is unset, such as `"weekly 1"` (rotate on Mondays) without `frequency`, or `"nocreate"` without `create_mode`.
- The file is written with mode `0644` and owned by the user running Terraform, because logrotate ignores configuration files that are writable by group or others, or owned by anyone but root or the user running it. A missing `/etc/logrotate.d` is created with mode `0755`.

## Validation

Everything that can be checked without logrotate is checked when Terraform plans, so that no attribute can add a block or a script to the file:

- `name` must be a plain file name that logrotate reads: letters, digits and `_.+@-`, not starting with `.`, `+`, `@` or `-`, and not ending with an extension that logrotate skips in included directories, such as `.bak`, `.disabled`, `.dpkg-old`, `.rpmnew`, `.rpmsave`, `.swp` or `~`.
- `paths` must be absolute, without quotes, backslashes, `{`, `}`, `#`, control characters, `//` or `.` and `..` components, and must not repeat.
- `postrotate` must not contain a line `endscript`, which would end the script early and turn the rest into directives.
- `extra_directives` must be single lines that are not comments and contain no `{` or `}`, and must not start a script (`prerotate`, `postrotate`, `firstaction`, `lastaction`, `preremove`) or be `include`.
- `create_owner` needs `create_mode`, and `create_owner` and `create_group` must be set together, as in logrotate's `create <mode> <owner> <group>`: logrotate 3.22 and later read `create <mode> <owner>` as an owner and a group.

Before the new file is renamed into place, it is checked with `logrotate -d` (debug mode, which changes nothing and uses no state file), if logrotate is installed on the host. If logrotate reports an error in the file, or a warning about one of its lines, such as an unknown directive, a bad argument or an unknown user or group in `create` or `su`, apply fails with its messages and the file on disk is left as it was. logrotate also reports log files it can't rotate, such as missing ones; those are not errors in the file and are ignored. Without logrotate the file is installed unchecked. Set `validate = false` to skip the check.

## Behavior

- **Create** refuses a file that already exists: destroying the resource would remove it. Import it instead.
- **Update** rewrites the file.
- **Destroy** removes the file. A symlink at the file is never written through or removed.

Writes are atomic: the new content goes to a temporary file in `/etc/logrotate.d`, which gets its mode and owner first and is renamed over the old file, keeping its SELinux label. Edits hold the provider's [shared-file lock](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/blechschmidt/sysutils/latest/docs#concurrency-and-locking), so a file is never written by two resources or Terraform runs at once.

With the provider's `root_dir` set, the file is `<root_dir>/etc/logrotate.d/<name>`, and `path` shows the path inside the tree. The log `paths` are written as given: they name the files of the system that boots from the tree. The `logrotate -d` check is skipped below `root_dir`, because logrotate would look up the users, groups and log files of the host rather than of the tree; programs in the tree are never run.

## Drift Detection

On refresh the provider reads the file. Any change to its content, such as an edited or added line, shows up in the plan as a change to `content`, as does a change of its mode or ownership, and the next apply writes the file again. A file removed outside Terraform is created again.

## Import

A drop-in can be imported by its name in `/etc/logrotate.d`:

```shell
# By the name of the file in /etc/logrotate.d. The file must hold a single
# block of log paths; its directives are read into the attributes.
terraform import sysutils_logrotate.myapp myapp
```

The file is parsed into the attributes: directives of typed attributes go there, and all others to `extra_directives`. Only files with a single block of log paths, and at most a `postrotate` script, can be imported; files with several blocks, global directives or other scripts are refused. Comments and formatting are not kept, so the first apply after an import rewrites the file in the resource's format.
